items.title: The Most Interesting Part of Your Life
items.description: Reinvention can often seem like an inevitable part of getting older. The midlife crisis is practically baked into the American life cycle, at least in popular culture—a moment that can yield a new career, a new marriage, or, at the very least, a flashy new car. The 1960s radical Jerry Rubin wrote in his memoir Growing (Up) at 37 that he needed a completely new belief system to bring him back from a crisis so deep that, as he put it, “I felt dead at 34.” For him, as for many, the idea of a clean break with the past felt not only appealing but necessary. But for those alarmed by the turbulence of midlife, the writer Valeria Luiselli’s novels offer a refreshingly different perspective. “I once read in a book by Saul Bellow that the difference between being alive and dead is just a matter of viewpoint,” the narrator of Luiselli’s debut novel, Faces in the Crowd , recalls. She goes on to explain that the “living look from the center outward, the dead from the periphery to some kind of center.” According to this worldview, the middle of life, far from a time to reset yourself, is the crux of human existence. And in Luiselli’s new novel, Beginning Middle End , it’s also where the messiest, most interesting, and most exciting parts of a story occur. Creatively speaking, Luiselli is a bit of a chameleon, one who could herself be mistaken for a serial reinventor. The daughter of a Mexican diplomat, she was educated in both English and Spanish. At the start of her career, she wrote in Spanish, but after settling in New York, she switched to English with Tell Me How It Ends , a 2017 book-length essay about her experience as a volunteer court interpreter for undocumented Central American children . She hasn’t published a book of nonfiction since, but she recently told El País that it took her years to determine whether Beginning Middle End would be a novel or an essay. The fineness of the line between the two genres indicates that in her work overall, change is a matter of gradations. The same is certainly true of this book. Beginning Middle End starts with its nameless, newly single narrator, a Mexican writer living in New York, embarking on a monthslong European trip with her preteen daughter. In theory, this is a fresh beginning post-divorce, but in truth, she’s still in the thick of things: busy worrying about her career, her aging mother, the fact that her daughter will never see her ex-stepbrother again. Luiselli describes her narrator’s age as a time when “what one sees on one side is one’s children walking into life, and then, on the other side, one’s parents on their way out. The middle, then, is a difficult vantage point, where life and death meet.” Still, the novel is an ode to middles. The narrator thinks longingly of starting anew, but in practice, she’s eager for her existence as a mother and writer to get dull and stable again. Her interest in ordinariness (she dreams of a new “routine, a sustained everydayness”) separates Beginning Middle End from other recent divorce novels, such as Miranda July’s All Fours or Claire Vaye Watkins’s I Love You But I’ve Chosen Darkness , in which a female protagonist stages an irrevocable break with their marriage and married self. [ Read: The female-midlife-crisis novel ] Luiselli’s heroine, by contrast, likes continuity. It’s telling that her trip turns out not to include much wandering, though that was her original plan. But after only a few pages of country-hopping, she and her daughter arrive in Sicily, where an acquaintance has offered to lend them an apartment and where the protagonist’s grandmother was originally from. The narrator reports that “as soon as we stepped off the airplane I felt a deep sense of home—past or future, I’m not sure.” Regardless, she decides to remain in Sicily, and what seemed like a road novel reveals itself to be about settling down. Luiselli’s narrator still wants to make a calm life with her daughter, and maybe with a man as well: The acquaintance is an occasional lover of hers, and she awaits his return with rising sexual anticipation. Rather than give up on romance or motherhood, she grabs on to them both. Yet the narrator still wants some change, even after she gives up on her vision of a summer spent bouncing from place to place. Once in Sicily, she and her daughter discuss reinvention often. They read Ovid’s Metamorphoses , and much of the novel is devoted to their quest to return a mosaic of the shape-shifting god Proteus that the narrator’s Sicilian grandmother stole from an archaeological site before immigrating to Mexico. While food shopping, they fixate on a sign on a fishmonger’s stall: Cu nasci tunnu un po’moriri pisci spada , it reads in Sicilian, which the narrator glosses as “if you are born being a tuna fish you can’t die a swordfish.” Both characters seem to bristle at this motto. The daughter’s reaction, in particular, suggests an impressively mature desire to embrace change rather than loathe it—no small feat for a girl who just lost her stepfather and stepbrother to a tough divorce. [ Read: A divorce memoir with no lessons ] As for the narrator, believing that a person can change is even more psychologically important in the aftermath of her marriage, which degraded into a brutality that she recalls as banal in its awfulness. To underscore this reality, Luiselli describes the abuse her character endured in vague, universal language, an attention-grabbing choice given that her prose is otherwise very precise. Her narrator doesn’t even mention her own ex-husband but alludes to “the men who caught us off guard, who escalated so slowly that we didn’t notice at first, because we trusted them, married them, spent a life with them.” What comes next, though the narrator continues to use us rather than I , is clearly an account of frequent marital rape. After her divorce, she tries to regain her “body before the soul of it was looted,” a search that gives a new weight to her desire to write. She knows that “the only thing that allows me to feel properly grounded in life, present in the present, is being in the middle of writing something that I cannot not write.” Both she and the reader can hope, if not trust, that if she’s present in the present, then her soul will return. Yet for much of the novel, the narrator is afraid that she is no longer capable of being active in her own life. She has no choice but to do so with her daughter and with her mother, who lives in Mexico and is showing early signs of memory loss. But creatively, she’s less certain. She struggles to concentrate on writing, and at an open-air performance of a Vivaldi opera, she quickly loses focus on the music and instead starts watching her fellow checked-out concertgoers. As she does, she wonders what it is “that allows some minds to catch the thread of a beginning and see it through, and others to lose it (or let it go) and not follow for any longer than a few minutes.” The answer—the ability and willingness to push through distraction to eventually create or appreciate art—is clearly relevant to novel writing, too. If you can’t sit, bored and likely miserable, with the start of a book, you have no way to get to the middle, which Luiselli refers to as the “place where the story simply has to continue.” Luiselli has long been intrigued by literary boredom. Beginning Middle End , like all of her novels, goes without what its protagonist calls the “corset of plot.” By no means does it lack drama—see: impending lover, maybe-sick mother; because this is Sicily, there’s also a looming volcano—but traditional story does not drive the novel forward. As it winds down, Luiselli does not resolve any of its questions (Is the mom all right? Will the narrator be able to write again?) but instead hands the narrative from the protagonist to her daughter. The novel’s final section takes on the daughter’s voice, and in its last lines, the daughter arbitrarily declares her mother’s book over: “This is the story,” she says. “It has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and this is the end.” By rejecting the myth of beginning again and the idea that endings are inherently meaningful, Luiselli highlights the fascination of the middle. It’s a bold approach to life, more than literature. In the traditional arc of a book, of course, the ending can come only once. A beginning, meanwhile, sets a story’s tone and stakes. It tells the audience whom and what to care about, and creates, ideally, a sense of expectation and intrigue. Beginnings, in short, exist to make you want to read middles. In life, this can be tougher to accept; it’s hard to be in the middle, twisting between life and death. Still, as my grandfather used to say, it beats the alternative. He was talking about dying, but also, I wouldn’t want to be (or have) a newborn forever, or ditch my husband after the honeymoon, or quit my job as soon as a challenge arises. Forging onward can sound duller and bleaker than launching a new life—hence, I think, the appeal of stories about multiverses—but in fact, it leads directly to the interesting stuff. Beginning Middle End knows that the first and last words in its title are just necessities. It’s the center, where life flails on, that counts.

items.title: The Masculinity Scam
items.description: A merican manhood is a fragile and precarious thing, shattered by the slightest deviation from ever-shifting norms—eating the wrong taco, tasting tofu, not eating meat, or maybe eating too much meat. Or at least, that is what right-wing commentators have suggested by their attacks on the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate in Texas, James Talarico. Since the 37-year-old state senator clinched the nomination, right-wing politicians and media figures have been running a bizarre smear campaign attacking Talarico for not being manly enough. President Donald Trump called Talarico a “vegan,” and Trump’s adviser Stephen Miller has twice declared that Talarico is “transgender.” Right-wing media figures have referred to him as “Tofu Talarico” and suggested that he is “against meat.” That prompted the Talarico campaign to put out photos of the candidate eating meat, leading the Fox News host Jesse Watters to sneer that Talarico was “getting his hands on whatever meat he can.” Watters is 48 years old. Anyway, you get it. Talarico is gay or something, and for the GOP, there’s definitely something wrong with that. Its own candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, is mired in allegations of corruption and infidelity, and is committed to some policies so extreme that, like Trump himself , they are unpopular even in deep-red Texas. Talarico’s choirboy looks and religiously inflected liberalism provide a stark contrast to Paxton’s hypocritical self-righteousness, and so Republicans are desperately trying to make those qualities seem like weaknesses. George W. Bush’s advisers snickered that John Kerry looked “French.” Trump, of course, is famous for put-downs whose cruelty is part of their appeal. But there’s something new about the attacks on Talarico. Calling a man “French” or “vegan” retains a mote of the old deniability. Calling Talarico “transgender” does not. The rhetoric resembles nothing more than the frothing tone of masculinity influencers in the online manosphere, with its strict but arbitrary standards for what makes a man a man. Although Republicans have devoted themselves to this type of marketing, parts of the Democratic coalition have an appetite for it as well —they’ve already face-Platnered at least once as a result. [ Listen: When both parties try to out-macho each other ] The Trump administration and the conservative movement seem to have taken this advertising strategy and transformed it into an ideology. The result is a secretary of health and human services who posts videos of himself working out in jeans and then presides over outbreaks of measles and explosive diarrhea; a director of Medicare and Medicaid who takes a break from stripping health care away from children to demonstrate how not to do a squat; and a defense secretary who interrupts his day job of starting and losing pointless, illegal wars in the Middle East to announce that he will force testosterone tests on service members. And Americans are supposed to be impressed by these overgrown children showing off their masculine prowess while failing at their basic adult responsibilities. A ny man who goes online today is apt to come across content telling him that he will never find a partner who will earn him the respect of other men if he lacks money and connections, if he is not bodybuilder-fit with a full head of hair, if he is not more than six feet tall. Online influencers who push this narrative have products to sell. They want you to buy their workout apps, their advice sessions, their investment plans. That’s just how a lot of advertising works: It makes you insecure so you’ll pay for a product in hopes of temporarily silencing your gnawing sense of inadequacy. Ad campaigns have long preyed in this way on female insecurities, telling women how they are supposed to look and act. In her 1991 book, Backlash , the feminist writer Susan Faludi observed that the rise of women in the workplace was a boon for the beauty industry. Women were told they needed to buy more makeup because they’d been masculinized by having a job: “Professional progress had downgraded their looks; equality had created worry lines and cellulite,” Faludi wrote. That marketing, though, was designed to turn women against themselves; the manosphere now tells men to lash out at others instead. It encourages white men in particular, but not exclusively, to blame their problems on a society that has allowed their lessers to compete with them for employment, power, and prestige by removing the barriers that once kept them out. The heroin-chic era was destructive for women, but it didn’t result in popular media figures advocating for men to be stripped of the right to vote. Notably, tradwife content, the ideological companion to manosphere content, is mostly about how wonderful it would be to be a kind of s lave . Social scientists have found that when men think their masculinity is being questioned, they may dismiss that challenge as irrelevant, they may quietly feel bad or insecure, or they may overcompensate by trying to behave in a more stereotypically masculine fashion. And that last reaction is where the dollars are. Be a man and buy a gun. Get the manly cereal for men. Wipe your butt with the wet wipes for men. Get the manly smelling deodorant. Eat the manly steak. It’s no coincidence that gambling apps and crypto companies have spent so much money on ads that make giving them your money seem adventurous. Just as the manosphere and its galaxy of hucksters want you to fork over your cash so you can feel better about yourself as a man, Republicans want to make you feel insecure about your masculinity so that you vote Republican. Masculinity, in this sense, is a lifestyle product: one that comes with a set of political beliefs predicated on the subjugation of women, minority groups, and anyone else who men are told are their inferiors. There’s inherently nothing wrong with masculinity itself. Boys and young men don’t seek out the manosphere “because they inherently hate women or think they are inferior,” the feminist writer Jessica Valenti has written . Rather, they “are desperate for community and answers in a confusing time of their lives.” When people are constantly told that the only way to be a worthwhile human being is to conform to gender norms, they will naturally strive to meet those expectations, even if it means being harsh to themselves or others. But the strength of those emotions is precisely what makes them so exploitable. Adam Stanaland, a psychology professor at the University of Richmond, told me that what’s concerning is when insecure men feel pressured to validate their manhood by harming others. Stanaland co-authored a study on “fragile” masculinity that notes that such men may compensate by endorsing “political bigotry, homophobia, sexual violence, and anti-environmentalism,” and that they are “more likely to endorse policies and politicians that disproportionately harm marginalized groups.” Stanaland speculated that for “white men especially, their masculinity is framed by this idea they must be at the top of not only the gender hierarchy, but also other social hierarchies, and so any kinds of threats to that positioning of them at the hierarchy could be responded to with these compensatory behaviors.” Sexist ideology nevertheless has a broader appeal. The former congressman Matt Gaetz, whose nomination for attorney general was derailed by allegations that he’d had sex with a minor (allegations that he denied), predicted before the 2024 election that “for every Karen we lose, there’s a Julio and a Jamal ready to sign up for the MAGA movement.” Ironically, some of the most prominent masculinity influencers are not themselves white. Andrew and Tristan Tate, who were recently arrested on rape and sex-trafficking charges after being spared from legal consequences for years thanks to interventions by the Trump administration, are biracial. This has not stopped the brothers from repeating racist far-right arguments that play well online, such as Andrew implying that Jews are “subverting western populations into mass genetic suicide.” This idea, known today as the “Great Replacement” theory, is a continuation of old-timey racist fears of “race mixing” (a common manosphere preoccupation )—and it’s a little weird to hear coming from a biracial man. One part of selling a product is knowing your customer base, I suppose. More than a decade ago, when I was first reporting on the manosphere, it was populated largely by middle-aged men, many of them divorcés, who retained a superficial concern for men’s welfare. They at least pretended that it was a normal political movement focused on issues such as suicide, rules disfavoring dads in custody battles, and male victims of domestic violence. They may have dreamed of forcing women back into traditional subservience—taking away female suffrage, repealing antidiscrimination laws, and making it harder for women to divorce—but mostly they avoided saying so out loud. Over the past 10 years, the misogyny of the manosphere has become more open and strident, but the big innovation seems to have been combining that conspiratorial misogyny with earnest self-help advice. Heartbreak and rejection leave people emotionally vulnerable, and the manosphere pitch often comes paired with benign advice about standing up for yourself, being mentally tough, or becoming physically active. But getting yourself together with the expectation that soon everyone you meet will be forced to respect you inevitably leads to disappointment. When that disappointment sets in, the manosphere has an explanation: Can’t find a girlfriend? It’s because women who make their own living can no longer be forced into marrying guys they don’t like. Can’t find a job? It’s because undeserving women and minorities are being picked instead of you, even though you’re better. Feel bad about yourself? It’s because our feminized society deprived you of a life of meaningful toil, military adventure, and elevated social status. It is a bleak view of the world, a kind of male doomerism in which a meaningful life can be found only in the domination and exploitation of others. The fact that none of that advice could ever help someone find real intimacy or success isn’t a problem for the manosphere hucksters, because those achievements would be bad for the business model. They prefer their followers to be tied only to them, forking over cash to be told they’re victims of one conspiracy after another. They’ll just tell you that women can’t be trusted because they are mere baubles to impress other men with, and other men cannot be trusted because they are the competition. There probably shouldn’t be a lot of overlap between religious-right leaders, government officials, and someone like Andrew Tate, who proudly describes himself as a “pimp.” Yet Tate’s belief that “society functions better as a patriarchy” is hard to distinguish from the views of Doug Wilson, the pastor invited by Hegseth to preach at the Pentagon , who thinks that women shouldn’t be allowed to vote . Pious or secular, these beliefs come down to the same idea: Men are people, and women are things. As my colleague Helen Lewis has reported , “Woman-bashing plays well on social media and sells lots of ads for crypto, sports betting, and supplements.” She adds: “You can make good money telling men that they’re the truly oppressed sex.” You can win a lot of votes that way, too. [ Russell Berman: The return of the Democratic manly man ] The logic of this male-doomer industry is to remove all unfair competition—from women, from minorities, from immigrants—by either disenfranchising or dispossessing them, and in this way reassert the dominance to which white American men are entitled. And even if you’re not white, wouldn’t it feel good to put all those women who don’t like you in their place? O ne prominent explanation for the resurgence of reactionary ideas about gender is that it’s a consequence of structural changes in the economy: Manly jobs such as manufacturing and construction have been lost, while feminine-coded service jobs such as caregiving have surged. This is an accurate description of what’s happened in the economy, but it’s not a sufficient explanation for the rise of extreme misogyny. For one thing, these economic changes are decades old. Faludi followed up Backlash with Stiffed , which argued that working-class American men were being deprived of work they could be proud of while still being expected to live up to a traditional idea of men as providers. Stiffed was published more than a quarter century ago. The theory also doesn’t necessarily line up with who is most likely to buy into what the manosphere is selling. “There’s this myth out there that the young men who are embracing this ideology and moving to the right in a coherent and virulent way are people being left behind by the economy,” John Ray, who does polling for the Young Men Research Project, told me. “Actually, a lot of the young men who have these more extreme right-wing views are more economically well-off than others in the sample.” The project’s polling, he said, has found that “young men who were more economically precarious, broadly speaking, were less ideological—one way or the other. It was actually young men that said that they were less worried about their finances who are more likely to have some of those right-wing views.” The modern data economy must play a bigger role. People spend more time than ever on their phones. Virtually everything you see while you are scrolling a social-media site is an advertisement—for a product, a lifestyle, or an individual feed. Social-media companies want you to be glued to your phone for as long as possible so they can sell you things or produce data they can sell to others. It doesn’t matter if the things you’re watching or reading are true or false, right or wrong. Extremism draws attention, so it’s not surprising that we’re seeing more extreme ideas about what it means to be a man. Yet when conservatives complain about diverse casting in movies, or romanticize the era of colonialism, or insist that women should be disenfranchised, this is more than mere trolling for eyeballs. They are telling you their policy plan. And they are using the psychological lever of male insecurity to win political support for that program. What kind of program has this internet-brain-rotted masculinity brought us? A public-health official who neglects fatal outbreaks of preventable diseases because he seems to believe that only the strong should survive . A Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War, that launches a needless war of choice in the Middle East. A government that props up the fossil-fuel industry (manly) while deliberately suppressing green alternatives (girly), leading to a catastrophic rise in energy prices when that war doesn’t go as planned. A president who imposed tariffs to bring back “manly jobs,” but only drove up inflation instead. It’s hard to see how any of this has made men’s lives better. But maybe making other people’s lives worse is enough.

items.title: The Return of the Monarch
items.description: Photographs and Videos by Ana Hop “ ¡Mire! ” My guide, Silvestre, pointed upward, as if I wasn’t already walking with my neck craned as far back as it could go. The sky was alive with millions of fluttering shapes, congregating into clouds at random, occasionally turning into ribbons that wound through the trees. So many butterfly wings beat the air that their vibrations were audible, like a waterfall rushing in the distance. I understood for the first time the immensity of the event I’d come to see. I was in the center of El Rosario butterfly sanctuary, part of Mexico’s Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. Unaccustomed to the thin air at nearly 11,000 feet above sea level, I’d ridden Pelucha, a rust-colored mare, to the heights of the reserve. About halfway up, the orange-and-black butterflies had begun appearing in groups, alighting on flowers or gathering to sip water from puddles. Coupled pairs mated everywhere, and their constant entanglements on the path made it difficult to avoid stepping on them; Pelucha happily crunched more than a few underfoot. I dismounted at the top of the trail and followed Silvestre as he ducked under a rope that kept tourists from accessing the most sensitive areas of the reserve. It was February, and the monarchs—northerners that had wintered in Mexico—were preparing for their final journey, which doubled as the first leg of a multigenerational relay race north. Their delicateness belies a life cycle that more resembles long-haul trucking than anything you might read in a children’s book. Each of the butterflies above me had already braved many grueling trials. In the following week or so, the majority would be on their way. Monarch migration is a wonder of the natural world, one of the longest annual cycles of movement undertaken by any creature on Earth, spanning thousands of miles. Over the past half century, the lands that the monarchs traverse have become more hostile to them, a result of development and herbicides, global warming and organized crime, all of which have put the future of that migration in doubt. And yet, the story I’d come to write—my reason for interloping in this and other sanctuaries—was not just a narrative of beauty being diminished by human trampling and greed. Recently, there’s been good news: Population estimates, after a long march downward, have been increasing for the past two years. This stabilization appears to be connected at least in part to efforts to save butterfly habitats in Mexico, the United States, and Canada. Those developments are reason to hope that there may still be a pathway left for saving the monarchs and their migration. The monarch persists partly because of the dogged work from its human partners; because of people who have given their life—in every sense of the phrase—to preserve nature. But mostly, the monarch persists because life’s job is to live; because within those thimble-size bodies hides a dynamo of survival that puts our most incredible machines to shame. The more we learn about the butterflies, the more we understand how extraordinary it is that they have so far beaten the odds we have stacked against them, and how forbidding those odds remain. Ana Hop for The Atlantic A monarch butterfly in El Rosario butterfly sanctuary, in Angangueo, Mexico We’ve known just how epic the monarch’s migration is for only about half a century. In the 1970s, using paper tags placed on butterflies’ wings, the Canadian butterfly researchers Fred and Norah Urquhart completed a lifelong mission to uncover the mystery of where all the monarchs born in Ontario went in the fall. To their surprise, the sojourners they followed made it all the way down the length of the U.S., and on to the mountain forests of Michoacán, Mexico. There they roosted, packed tightly into just a handful of colonies that collectively cover no more than a few city blocks, yet hold nearly all of the continent’s monarchs in winter. The Urquharts first visited these colonies in 1976, and National Geographic published a cover story on their breakthrough. For centuries, Indigenous people in Mexico’s highlands have witnessed the monarchs’ annual return during harvest season, though for most of that time they didn’t know where they came from. The butterflies have been making this migration for as long as 20 millennia, once finding paths to and from the fields gouged out by glaciers retreating with the spring during the last Ice Age. Now their roosting grounds sit within a handful of sanctuaries that I visited. At Sierra Chincua, a few miles north of El Rosario, I stood on a cliff overlooking the slender trunks of oyamel fir trees. I watched living streams of monarchs flying in different directions, sometimes winding about one another like a gigantic knot forever being tied, and looked in vain for three monarchs that I knew were in the fray. Each had been given a designation in a spreadsheet—CHI016, CHI013, and CHI001—but those were all very boring names for butterflies, so I’d asked my 6-year-old daughter to give them better ones. She’d come up with Cinderella, Eric, and Carle. (She knows The Very Hungry Caterpillar by heart.) Nothing about the trio was unusual, save for the gear they wore. Affixed to each butterfly’s thorax, like a tiny backpack, was a transmitter the size of a grain of rice. These transmitters, called BlūMorpho tags, had been developed by a company called Cellular Tracking Technologies , and Cinderella, Eric, and Carle were part of the first generation of monarchs to wear them. Before my visit to the sanctuaries, I’d spoken with David La Puma, an executive at CTT and one of the brains behind the BlūMorpho. The company had initially focused on developing tech for tracking eagles, but La Puma had previously worked in monarch conservation, and carried his interest in the butterflies with him. Tracking a monarch is different from tracking an eagle, as monarchs each weigh less than a dollar bill. Any transmitter attached to one could weigh no more than a few grains of sand. No battery could be made that small and still provide power over months of flying, and the solar panels that CTT used for eagle trackers were much too heavy. But the team figured out a solution: taking the ultrathin solar squares that line the wings of satellites and carefully chopping them up into tiny bespoke cells. An early version of the tracker, applied to butterflies with dabs of eyelash glue, was linked with a cellphone app via Bluetooth, allowing enthusiasts to follow nearby butterflies—a sort of “Pokémon Go for monarchs,” La Puma said—and record their locations in somewhat haphazard fashion. The newest iteration works more like Google Maps, providing far more complete data on the butterflies’ locations to anyone, almost in real time. Knowing more about butterflies’ individual habits may enable us to help them thrive collectively (more on that later). The data also just help us get to know the monarchs better. As it turns out, some seem to be worse with directions than others, and can find themselves traveling west or south from Mexico. In the prototyping stage, some monarchs were detected near oil platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, nowhere near land, and some butterflies appeared to enjoy Caribbean vacations. Yet the majority seem to follow well-established paths along invisible corridors in the air. Cinderella, Eric, and Carle had all been tagged in Sierra Chincua, which meant that I could deduce certain facts about their lives. They were already bona fide world-class wanderers, having flown there all the way from Canada in the fall, a three-month trip. Along the way, they’d dodged birds and windmills and cars, eventually reaching the same patch of forest—perhaps even the same trees—that their great-grandparents had roosted in. For much of the winter, they had not eaten and had barely moved, jamming themselves so tightly against their fellow travelers that from a distance they looked like scales armoring the sides of the trees. Now they’d awakened, stretching their wings and warming up. Ana Hop for The Atlantic Monarchs at rest on tree branches at El Rosario in early March. In winter’s colder temperatures, the butterflies pack themselves together so tightly that they resemble scales on the trees. Though I couldn’t spot them in the sky, I could see from my phone that Cinderella, Eric, and Carle were near. Over the next several weeks, I would keep tabs on them, following their movements with a level of detail that would have been impossible only a year ago. Individual butterflies can travel as far as 100 miles in a single day and can congregate in groups so thick that they show up as clouds on weather radar. Glider pilots have seen them flying at altitudes above 10,000 feet. Year after year, new generations tend to gather around the same landmarks, despite having never seen them before. They seem, for example, to love the Barnegat Lighthouse on Long Beach Island, in New Jersey. The monarchs’ feats of navigation are enabled by their internal technology, a set of instinctual tools that in some ways surpasses our understanding. The butterflies’ eyes can sense the angle and intensity of different forms of light. In each antenna, a complex series of molecules maintains their circadian clock , which, when combined with sunlight cues, gives them their sense of direction. When the sun is unreliable, monarchs have a secondary method of pathfinding— a biological compass that allows them to sense Earth’s magnetic field. Internal thermostats help govern the timing of their northward movements. The butterflies’ migration evolved to fit North America’s geography. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, which grows best in cooler climates, but the butterflies can’t tolerate freezing temperatures. The length of the continent’s interior, unbroken by mountains or oceans, allows the monarchs to find the right weather and plants throughout the year—a Goldilocks ecology, neither too hot nor too cold. They are a marvel of nature’s engineering, of the kind of elegance that evolution can achieve over deep time. “Winter is hard for insects that have to survive it, and monarchs basically avoid it by leaving,” says Karen Oberhauser, a researcher at the University of Wisconsin at Madison and a co-founder of the Monarch Butterfly Fund. Unlike many other butterfly species, which are adapted to very specific microbiomes, monarchs have options if a local environment changes. Indeed, they seem strikingly well adapted for living alongside the world’s most disruptive change agent: humanity. Milkweed tends to thrive in transitional areas, such as fallow fields, unkempt lawns, and the edges of highways. “When I first started studying monarchs, it really did seem like they kind of had an advantage over a lot of other species,” Oberhauser told me. “That’s a disturbance-adapted species.” She said, affectionately, that monarchs are like rats or pigeons, all part of the strange but sturdy menagerie of modern life. But there are limits to any creature’s adaptability, and human activity has steadily eroded the monarch’s margin for error. In the 1930s, Mexico’s land-reform program created ejidos , areas designated for communal use by peasants. They began clearing the ancient oyamel forests to plant corn, beans, and squash, and sold the felled timber. Commercial interests also stepped in, accelerating logging in the butterfly’s winter habitats. North of the Rio Grande, there have been disturbances to the disturbances. Although milkweed can flourish along roads, the advent of the interstate system also introduced one of the most efficient killers of butterflies: speeding traffic. And although farmland in the Midwest was once a reliable (if accidental) incubator for milkweed, the development of Roundup Ready crops in the ’90s allowed more promiscuous use of herbicides. Almost overnight, milkweed disappeared from large-scale farms. According to a recent report from the World Wildlife Fund, the total area covered by monarch colonies in winter decreased from 45 acres in 1996 to a low of fewer than two acres in 2013. The five-year average of colony size has dropped by 80 percent since the mid-’90s, a plunge of some 170 million butterflies. As Oberhauser told me, the changes wrought by humans have caught up to the monarchs. In fact, the complexity of the migration might now be a liability, as multiple stops on the journey face upheaval at once. “What makes them so strong also makes them vulnerable,” she said. My trio of butterflies had been strong from their beginnings. As caterpillars, they’d gorged on milkweed, a plant that is toxic to most animals, and incorporated its poison into their bodies. Their distinct coloring is both a warning for predators and a badge of initiation. They are already one-percenters—only one in 100 of the eggs laid in Ontario last year had produced butterflies that made it this far. Their generation, called a “super-generation,” is bigger and more robust than their parents’ was or their children’s will be: They are centurions built to make the journey all the way south and partway back. (Two successive generations will eventually complete the round trip to Canada.) Now, after a winter of fasting, huddled close against the cold, they are regaining their strength, sipping nectar from flowers near their roosting trees. On my phone, I can see a map with each location that the butterflies ping as they meander from place to place, ever returning to their central roosts. My phone shows only their movements, not their more private matters, but I know that before they leave these forests behind, they will each find a mate. For Cinderella and Eric—which, as I told my daughter, is a female butterfly—their mates’ package of sperm will also contain a deposit of nutrients that will help them handle the rigors of the trip. Carle will weaken himself, giving his mate a gift that she must use to ensure the survival of their offspring. For the past several decades, a diverse group of grassroots activists, scientists, and enthusiasts has worked to forestall the monarchs’ decline. I’d come to Sierra Chincua as the guest of one of them. José Luis Álvarez Alcalá, a local activist and farmer, showed me around. He pointed to the visitors’ center, restaurants, and gift shops near the sanctuary’s entrance. “None of this was here 30 years ago,” he told me. Then he pointed to a copse of young trees creeping up the hills. “A lot of that wasn’t either.” Álvarez Alcalá would know: He helped create much of it. Ana Hop for The Atlantic José Luis Álvarez Alcalá at Hacienda la Cruz, his home and tree nursery Years of chain-smoking can be heard in the thickness of Álvarez Alcalá’s voice, and when we met, he sported a limp from a recent fall while working. He wasn’t originally a butterfly guy, he said, but was interested in revitalizing the region that encompassed the sanctuaries, and he ran a tree nursery on Hacienda la Cruz, a 17th-century Spanish colonial estate that he’d restored. By the 1980s, just a few years after the National Geographic story came out, the monarchs were already drawing streams of intrepid sightseers from abroad, despite almost no tourism infrastructure. Álvarez Alcalá realized that there might be a way to align the survival of the species with the local economy. In 1986, President Miguel de la Madrid gave national protections to the main colony sites, creating the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. But those protections did not halt or even slow logging. Encouraged by the butterfly scientist Lincoln P. Brower, Álvarez Alcalá and his associates came up with a more proactive plan. They would give the members of the ejidos oyamel fir and pine saplings to grow, instead of their usual crops. The growers would still be free to profit from their land by selling timber for Christmas trees, lumber, or charcoal, but would be encouraged to harvest the wood sustainably. If done right, on a wide-enough scale, the model could help provide both income for the ejidatarios and the basis for butterfly tourism. Álvarez Alcalá says that, since launching in 1997, his La Cruz Habitat Protection Project has planted about 20 million oyamel fir and pine trees. Other groups have also reforested hundreds of hectares. The oldest of the trees planted as part of this experiment are now maturing and providing winter homes for exhausted monarchs. Over the span of just a few years, reforesting and ecotourism have transformed much of Michoacán, the state in which the sanctuaries reside. In the municipality of Angangueo, a brilliant mural depicts the social history of the monarchs, the “ hijas del sol ,” including a painting of the now-famous 1976 National Geographic cover. In El Rosario, the trinkets and souvenirs, the tour-bus parking lots, and even the stable of horses for rent all speak to a symbiosis that has only recently come to be. Ana Hop for The Atlantic An ecotourism industry has developed around El Rosario. Rental horses and guides help tourists travel along the reserve’s high mountain trails. The monarch’s star turn has changed the places along the more northerly parts of its route as well. In the U.S., seven states list the monarch as their official insect or butterfly, and in many places, monarchs appear on license plates that urge fellow drivers to protect the environment. More than 50,000 yards, parks, and schools now feature Monarch Waystations, special gardens stocked with milkweed and flowers. According to the World Wildlife Fund, the overwintering areas covered by monarchs this year increased by 64 percent. Cinderella, Eric, and Carle’s generation was the largest to leave Mexico in seven years. The measured takeaway from the WWF is that “despite challenges, conservation efforts are making a difference.” Yet there are new challenges, new crises in front of the monarchs. And these may eclipse the ones they’ve seen so far. “Fucking avocados.” Álvarez Alcalá’s son Luca was driving me around the outskirts of Hacienda la Cruz, where La Cruz Habitat Protection Project is based. He pointed to the offending field in the distance, its neat rows of hunter-green bushes a dead giveaway. The fruits represented one of the emerging threats to the reforesting mission, and to the monarch’s survival. I’d arrived in Mexico just after the annual high-water mark for avocado consumption : the Super Bowl. Michoacán is the largest avocado-growing region in the world, producing nearly all avocados eaten in the United States. Its volcanic soil is ideal for the fruit, and intense American demand for guacamole and fancy toast has, in these parts, given avocados the moniker oro verde —“green gold.” Unfortunately for monarchs, their forests sit right in the middle of some of the most promising areas for growing avocados. And the green-gold rush is so lucrative that it has drawn the attention of the area’s cartels, which now extort local growers, smuggle many of their avocados across the border, and even operate plantations directly. There’s a good chance that if you bought chips and guac to eat while you watched Bad Bunny during the big game, a cartel profited. Recently, cartels have been a major force behind illicit logging in the forests that Álvarez Alcalá and his son have tried to revive and protect, and much of the land has been converted for avocado farming. In 2020, Homero Gómez González, a prominent conservationist at the Biosphere Reserve, was found dead in Ocampo, the closest municipality to the sanctuary. Gómez González had been known as a vociferous antagonist of loggers. His killing has not been solved, but many outlets have placed the blame on the cartels. Those same cartels instigated the crisis that gripped Mexico during my travels. Just three days before I got to Hacienda la Cruz, Mexican authorities killed Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes , the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. The death of “El Mencho” sparked violence across the states of Jalisco and Michoacán: Cartel members erected barricades on major roads and ambushed National Guard members, killing at least 25 and also attacking several journalists. When I asked the elder Álvarez if touring the region would be safe, he gave perhaps the least-encouraging encouragement I’d ever heard: “I think there will be no problems,” he said. “But nothing in life is for sure.” During my trips to El Rosario and Sierra Chincua, both sanctuaries were mostly empty of tourists; cartels had been burning cars near the base of Sierra Chincua. It was all a stark reminder of how precarious monarch tourism is, and how much money there is to be made in destruction. Ana Hop for The Atlantic So many butterflies congregate along El Rosario’s high mountain trails that the vibration of their flapping wings can be audible to the human ear. When I spoke with Megan Fulton, the executive director of Álvarez Alcalá’s project, she was keen to point me to a recent report from the WWF showing that, the avocado boom notwithstanding, rates of forest degradation and illegal logging in the sanctuaries have slowed in the past year. She attributed the positive development to the local communities being galvanized by global warming and weather changes. “They are the communities that are already seeing the effects of climate change,” she said. “So they want to restore their land and protect it for future generations.” But the very fact that the communities are experiencing tangible effects— unprecedented heat waves that have killed hundreds, record droughts and wildfires that have ruined crops—means that the problem is bigger than organized crime, and perhaps beyond the ability of individual people or local groups to solve. Climate change is an accelerant for troubles that are already afoot. High mountain elevations that were once cool and less hospitable for avocado growing are getting hotter—and thus more tempting for felling. Warmer temperatures will also narrow the already tiny bands of habitability for oyamel firs, disrupting forest ecologies even in places that logging hasn’t yet touched. [ From the December 2025 issue: Vann R. Newkirk II on what climate change will do to America by mid-century ] The most ominous signs were visible from Hacienda la Cruz. In the forests just outside the property, like scars on the green mountainside, three ugly patches of brown, bare tree skeletons stood out. Luca explained that these patches had been infested by pine bark beetles, notorious evergreen-killers that feed on stressed or weakened conifers. The beetles are a normal part of forest ecosystems, and their numbers are usually controlled by cold winters. But the season has grown warmer. More trees now suffer from heat stress and dehydration, making them targets. Oyamels are particularly vulnerable. Authorities have already been forced to cut down whole sectors of the reserve to keep beetle infestations from spreading. On my phone, I can see that by mid-February, Cinderella is restless, regularly streaming to the southwest and back, even visiting Ocampo once or twice, veering toward Loncheria Los 4 Elementos, a little snack bar in town that sells tortas, burgers, and micheladas. Eric is a bit more adventurous, making her way almost as far west as Ciudad Hidalgo, where the great father of the nation once owned a hacienda. Carle is more of a homebody, sticking closer to Sierra Chincua and often staying in its forests. Eric is the first of the trio to leave for good, but her eagerness might be her undoing—the weather might not yet be warm enough for a successful transit. She flies north through Querétaro, but then her tracker stops transmitting. Cinderella and Carle choose to leave with the bulk of their cohort a week later, around the second week of March. There’s not much road ahead for Carle; he stops transmitting soon after. Chase Castor for The Atlantic A University of Kansas student, Merrie Clough, prepares caterpillar food, which will be sent, along with larvae, to individuals and schools hoping to raise monarch butterflies. Chase Castor for The Atlantic A paper tracking tag being affixed to a monarch at Monarch Watch, a hub of butterfly research and conservation in Lawrence, Kansas. But Cinderella keeps going, winding her way through Querétaro, swerving toward the old colonial city of San Miguel de Allende, then bending northeast. On March 15, she crosses the Rio Grande in the vicinity of Rio Grande City, Texas. The same week that Cinderella and her fellow survivors began fanning out into the United States, I visited Monarch Watch, an organization based at the University of Kansas that has long served as a hub of monarch research and conservation. I met Kristen Baum, its current director, and Chip Taylor, its founder and director emeritus. Baum runs a blog for Monarch Watch that tracks the radio-tagged butterflies’ movements. These data points could help conservationists model the migration more accurately, anticipate changes in population size, and better decide how and where to allocate resources to restore habitats. The day before my visit, Baum noted that CHI016, Cinderella’s government name, was likely the farthest north among all the tags. The tiny building that Monarch Watch occupies is jam-packed with records, research, and the butterflies themselves. In one room, I watched as a female split open her green chrysalis and emerged to spread her wings. Across the hall were refrigerators full of milkweed seeds—the group has donated more than 1 million milkweed plants for restoration projects since 2015. Taylor himself developed an artificial diet that could be used to raise caterpillars in lieu of live milkweed. In 2009, Monarch Watch sent caterpillars provisioned with this food (which looks something like old guacamole) on the Space Shuttle Atlantis to the International Space Station, where they successfully metamorphosed into butterflies. Chase Castor for The Atlantic A butterfly habitat box, used to transport monarch caterpillars from the center to the International Space Station in 2009 The word emeritus doesn’t capture the full role that Taylor, 88, still plays; he is a constant presence around the building. Before he secured more generous funding, he’d bankrolled many of Monarch Watch’s activities himself, using the proceeds from investments that he and his wife had made in Apple. He helped pay 100-peso rewards for finding paper butterfly tags—still the standard, low-tech method of tracking the creatures—in Mexico, which became a problem one year when people recovered more than 3,000 tagged butterflies. “That cost me $12,000,” he told me. “I wasn’t too anxious to do that over and over again.” It was hard, there in the middle of all of the butterfly posters and joyful pictures, to ask him the question I’d really come to ask. But Taylor eventually sighed and launched into an answer on his own. “What we’re doing ecologically to save the monarch butterfly, the scale of it is just nothing compared to what’s going on,” he said. “The population is going to creep lower and lower in time because we’re incapable, I think, at this point, of really mastering enough of the restoration.” In the United States and Canada, the math leads to a similar place as it does in Mexico. For all the bootstrapped recent successes in forestalling the butterfly’s decline, we’ve merely been playing catch-up. Now climate change is the primary threat to monarch numbers, and it is implacable. Higher temperatures make monarchs more susceptible to infection by a protozoan called Ophryocystis elektroscirrha , a parasite that drains the butterfly’s strength and makes it less likely to complete its journeys. And climate shifts are yet another threat to milkweed’s viability in particular locales, throwing off the distances and timing that are so crucial to each butterfly’s travels. “Maybe we can do something about the climate, but the opportunities for doing that are really, really diminishing very rapidly,” Taylor said. Even accounting for this year’s surprising bounce-back in numbers, he puts the timeline at 20 years or so before the migrating monarch’s numbers become too low to recover. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates upwards of a 50 percent chance that the eastern migratory monarchs will be extinct by 2080. When I was growing up, the flowers outside my bedroom window always brought visitors. I’d often wake up in the morning to the buzzing of a hummingbird’s wings. But the visitors I greeted most joyfully were the monarchs. On late-summer days, kaleidoscopes of butterflies would land together, covering the flowers like an orange blanket. Even then, I understood that there was something special about their fleeting delicateness. And fleeting it was: The world will probably never again see as many monarchs as existed then. But I would not bet entirely against the monarch. The fight to protect the species continues. In its persistence and its cooperative nature, that fight shares qualities with the monarch itself. The project is proof, in a fractured time, that people can join together and decide to help defend the things they see as valuable. Even as Taylor despaired of the monarch’s future, he mused, briefly, about the possibility of restocking wild-butterfly populations using a scaled-up version of Monarch Watch’s colony program. With that, his exertions in perfecting his homegrown colony process—the green smoothie for caterpillars, testing procedures for parasites—came into clearer view for me. They could be understood, I realized, as the beginnings of an attempt to bottle a fragment of the monarch’s magic for the future world. Maybe migration will continue, in that future, with an assist from something like a butterfly doomsday vault. Or maybe the next generation of the monarch’s friends will find further innovations to defeat problems that now seem insurmountable. The things we have learned recently about individual butterflies will be helpful for vanquishing those scientific problems, but the most important contribution of all this new information might be wonder itself. I am not a scientist, but after watching and tracking the butterflies for months, it seems to me that monarchs have something of a personality , a level of individuality that might endear them even more to the public. Some appear impulsive, or impressively rangy, leaving earlier and traveling more, whereas others fail to leave altogether. In El Rosario, when I asked Silvestre, my guide, about why groups of butterflies chose specific times to find water, he was enigmatic: “They decide.” And whether or not we call it personality, there’s science behind the idea of the butterflies’ individuality. In humans, traits such as neuroticism and recklessness appear to have some evolutionary basis—emerging perhaps to provide our species with sentries who alerted us to threats, and with explorers who led the way to new food sources. Research suggests that the goofball butterflies that might seem to lack a sense of direction are actually pioneers, scouts finding new habitats to exploit or new places to hunker down should worse come to worst. No matter what happens along the Mexico route, the monarch is likely to live on, albeit in smaller numbers, elsewhere. Across the planet, most populations of monarch butterflies—in Spain, in Hawaii—are likely descended from vagrants that veered off the Mexico migration path. Monarchs introduced to Australia in the 1870s have now established an annual migration along the east and southwest coasts—they have earned the fitting local epithet of “wanderers.” And in little pockets of the United States, Central America, and the Caribbean, in places where milkweed grows year-round, small monarch populations have settled in, no longer migrating and now sporting shorter wingspans than their more transient cousins. For all their seeming fragility, monarchs will be an extraordinarily capable partner in efforts to save them. They may yet surprise us. We may yet surprise ourselves. Cinderella is a marathoner. She flies through San Antonio and then skirts Austin, avoiding the congestion of the city proper during the South by Southwest festival, and then cuts through the Piney Woods toward Texarkana. At the time of her last detection, Cinderella is in Arkansas, having likely traveled from the Great Lakes to the Mexican highlands, and then halfway back. The diaspora she belongs to has spread out across a wide expanse of the country, ending up in Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and every place in between. They’ve spent themselves, but they have fulfilled their biological missions. During her roughly eight-month life, Cinderella traveled farther than scientists might have imagined possible, more than 3,000 miles as the butterfly flies. Along the way, she likely glued hundreds of tiny eggs onto milkweed plants. Perhaps some of the hatchlings will live, and continue her line. Perhaps they, too, will have her preternatural strength and tenacity. I hope, for the sake of my own daughter, and her ability to live in a world of beauty, that they will. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “How Do Monarchs Do It? ”

items.title: Remaniement gouvernemental en Guinée : Mamadi Doumbouya reconduit Bah Oury [Par Aboubacar Sakho]
items.description: Le Président de la République, SEM Mamadi Doumbouya, a procédé ce lundi 27 juillet 2026 à un remaniement partiel du gouvernement. Si le Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah conserve la tête de l'équipe gouvernementale, ce réaménagement est marqué par le maintien de plusieurs figures clés de l'exécutif, mais aussi par l'arrivée de nouvelles personnalités à la tête de départements stratégiques. Ce remaniement intervient dans un contexte où les autorités poursuivent la restructuration de l'appareil d'État. Plusieurs ministres sont reconduits dans leurs fonctions, tandis que d'autres changent de portefeuille ou font leur entrée au sein du gouvernement. Parmi les principales nouveautés figurent la nomination de Bintou Keita, ancienne représentante spéciale du Secrétaire général des Nations Unies au Congo, au ministère de l'Éducation nationale, de l'Alphabétisation, de l'Enseignement technique et de la Formation professionnelle. Aboubacar Kourouma, jusque-là Secrétaire général du ministère de la Fonction publique, prend les rênes du ministère de l'Industrie et du Commerce. De son côté, Lansana Béa Diallo revient à la jeunesse. Le chef du gouvernement, Amadou Oury Bah, reste en poste, confirmant la confiance que lui accorde le chef de l'État pour poursuivre la mise en œuvre des réformes engagées. items.title: Burkina Faso : Rasmané Pagbelguem devient docteur en mathématiques appliquées avec la mention Très honorable
items.description: Rasmané Pagbelguem a soutenu avec succès sa thèse de doctorat en Recherche opérationnelle, ce 27 juillet 2026. À l'issue de sa présentation, le jury lui a attribué la mention très honorable, le élevant ainsi au grade de docteur. C’est dans l’option Mathématiques appliquées que Rasmané Pagbelguem a mené ses travaux en vue de l’obtention du grade de docteur, spécialité Recherche opérationnelle. Ses recherches ont porté sur l’ « Investigation d’une nouvelle procédure métrique et implémentation de quelques méthodes de vote basées sur des métriques ». Il a inscrit sa recherche dans le domaine de l’aide à la décision. « Nous développons des méthodes qui pourront aider les décideurs à prendre une décision efficace. On applique ces méthodes pour pouvoir prendre une bonne décision, donc une décision rationnelle. On peut en démontrer l’efficacité. », a-t-il expliqué. Les résultats qu’il a développés peuvent s’appliquer notamment à la passation des marchés publics, aux processus électoraux, ainsi qu'à la sélection dans le domaine agricole. À l’issue d'un exposé de 40 minutes et de la phase de questions-réponses, son travail a été jugé recevable par le jury qui lui a décerné la mention très honorable. Pagbelguem Rasmané a inscrit sa recherche dans le domaine de l’aide à la décision En termes d’innovations, cette réflexion a permis de concevoir des méthodes faciles d’usage, qui contribueront à l’aide à la décision grâce à leur intégration dans un logiciel . « Le système de vote actuel étant sujet à la manipulation et à la corruption, lorsque les autorités passeront au vote par évaluation, la nouvelle méthode déjà existante pourra être appliquée », a-t-il déclaré, en ajoutant que ces méthodes seront intégrées sous forme de logiciels pour aider à réduire les coûts des élections. Selon le président du jury, Pr Blaise Somé, ce travail est d’une belle facture. Il a exprimé son appréciation pour la qualité du document et de l’exposé. « C’est de très bonne qualité. Le sujet est extrêmement important et porte sur la théorie du choix social, une théorie que tout le monde vit au quotidien. Ce travail est donc innovant, car il a réussi à concevoir de nouveaux algorithmes qu’il a implémentés avec le logiciel Python pour tirer des conclusions généralisables. », a-t-il apprécié. Selon le président du jury, Pr Blaise Somé, ce travail est d’une belle facture. Il a exprimé son appréciation pour la qualité du document et de l’exposé. Il a cependant fait un constat sur la présentation. « Il faut arriver à faire en sorte que le public qui sort d’ici tire quelque chose de la soutenance, qu’il apprenne quelque chose. », a-t-il noté. Les travaux de recherche du docteur Pagbelguem ont été dirigés par le Dr Zenabou Séré/Savadogo. « Compte tenu de son assiduité et de son sérieux, nous avons réussi à organiser la soutenance dans les délais impartis. C’est un étudiant engagé qui sait ce qu’il veut », a-t-elle déclaré. Les travaux de recherche du docteur Pagbelguem ont été dirigés par le Dr Zenabou Séré/Savadogo. items.title: Zinedine Zidane, premier sélectionneur franco-algérien à la tête de l’équipe de France
items.description: Ce qui était dans l’air depuis plusieurs mois est désormais officiel. Zinedine Zidane est le nouveau sélectionneur de l’équipe de France de football, en remplacement de Didier Deschamps, qui a quitté son poste à l'issue de la Coupe du monde 2026 après 14 ans à la barre technique des Bleus. C’est la première fois qu’un Franco-Algérien occupe une telle responsabilité au sein du football français. Zizou, qui s’est engagé pour quatre ans, a été présenté ce mardi 28 juillet au cours d'une conférence de presse au siège de la Fédération française de football (FFF). Zidane coach des Bleus pour 4 ans, jusqu’au Mondial 2030 “J'ai le privilège, le grand honneur et aussi l'émotion de vous dire que Zidane sera le prochain sélectionneur de l'équipe de France pour les 4 années qui viennent, qui couvriront les qualifications de la Ligue des nations, de l'Euro 2028 et de la Coupe du monde 2030”, a indiqué le président de la FFF, Philippe Diallo. Le contrat du nouveau sélectionneur prendra effet à partir du 1er août et le héros du Mondial 1998 présentera son staff début septembre, a-t-il précisé. Le premier match de l’équipe de France version Zinedine Zidane est prévu le 25 septembre face à la Turquie en Ligue des nations. Diallo a révélé que les contacts avec Zidane remontent à un an et demi, lorsque Deschamps avait émis le vœu de partir après le Mondial 2026. « Dès février 2025, j'ai rencontré Zinédine Zidane. J'ai pris contact avec lui pour lui proposer une mission à la tête de notre équipe de France. » Depuis, les deux hommes se sont vus à plusieurs reprises. C'est “la rencontre de deux envies”, a expliqué le président de la FFF. “Une envie parce que Zinédine est une des légendes du football français et, depuis de nombreuses années, il avait fait savoir qu'un de ses rêves était de diriger l'équipe de France. Et du côté de la Fédération, une envie d'avoir quelqu'un, qui après cette décennie magnifique, ait l'aura, la compétence, le cœur de nos fans et des Français pour diriger une des meilleures formations du monde.” “Président, je sais comment gagner », a dit Zidane au président de la Fédération. « J'ai su tout de suite que son envie correspondait aux besoins de la Fédération. Les choses se sont faites très vite et naturellement, l'évidence l'imposait », a dit Philippe Diallo. “C’est la seule chose que je voulais faire” Champion du monde en 1998 avec la France, Zidane a arrêté sa carrière en 2006. Comme entraîneur, il a connu un énorme succès avec le Real Madrid, qu’il a mené à trois victoires consécutives en Ligue des Champions d’Europe entre 2016 et 2018. C’est sa seule expérience en tant que coach. Zidane n’a pas entraîné depuis 2021, et beaucoup ont estimé qu’il attendait que la place de sélectionneur des Bleus se libère, ce qu’il a confirmé sans ambages ce mardi. “C’est juste une continuité, quelque part un rêve. J’ai eu des propositions ces 4-5 ans pour reprendre des clubs et je les ai toutes refusées pour l’équipe de France. C’est la seule chose que je voulais faire après mon expérience avec le Real Madrid”, a-t-il dit. “Je vais tout donner pour que cette équipe continue à gagner, la seule chose qui m'anime, c'est de pouvoir travailler pour cette équipe de France”, a insisté celui qui est considéré comme le meilleur footballeur français de tous les temps. Zinedine Zidane, âgé de 54 ans, est né en France de parents algériens. Toute sa famille est très attachée à l’Algérie. Son fils Luca est, depuis octobre 2025, le gardien de but des Verts. Lors de la CAN 2025 et du Mondial 2026, Zizou a fait le déplacement au Maroc et aux États-Unis pour suivre les matchs de son fils et de l'équipe d’Algérie. « L'équipe de France, c'est la seule chose que je voulais faire » Zinédine Zidane, nouveau sélectionneur de l'équipe de France pic.twitter.com/z38deVAUmo — L'Équipe (@lequipe) July 28, 2026 L’article Zinedine Zidane, premier sélectionneur franco-algérien à la tête de l’équipe de France est apparu en premier sur TSA .

Plus de 65 000 bacheliers sont attendus sur les différents sites pour un mois de formation axé sur le patriotisme, la discipline, la résilience et le sens des responsabilités. À travers cette initiative, le Burkina Faso fait le choix de former une jeunesse consciente de ses responsabilités, attachée aux valeurs nationales et préparée à contribuer pleinement à la construction d’un pays digne, libre et souverain. DCRP/Primature

items.title: Le Conseil national de concertation et de coopération des ruraux plaide pour une gouvernance agricole plus inclusive
items.description: Le Conseil national de concertation et de coopération des ruraux (CNCR) a participé, lundi 27 juillet 2026, à une réunion stratégique avec le ministère de l'Agriculture, de la Souveraineté alimentaire et de l'Élevage. Cette concertation, réunissant les organisations professionnelles des 14 régions du Sénégal, vise à renforcer la participation des producteurs à l'élaboration des politiques agricoles. Le président du Conseil national de concertation et de coopération des ruraux (CNCR), Nadjirou Sall, a pris part, lundi, à une réunion de concertation stratégique présidée par le ministre de l'Agriculture, de la Souveraineté alimentaire et de l'Élevage, Dr Cheikhou Oumar Bâ, en présence du ministre délégué chargé de l'Élevage, Me Ousmane Diagne. Cette rencontre a réuni les organisations professionnelles de producteurs et d'opérateurs agricoles des 14 régions du Sénégal. Elle s'inscrit dans une démarche visant à placer davantage les acteurs du monde rural au cœur de l'élaboration des politiques publiques agricoles. Des priorités identifiées pour le secteur Les échanges ont porté sur plusieurs enjeux jugés prioritaires par les participants. Il s'agit notamment de l'amélioration des mécanismes de subvention, du développement des chaînes de valeur, de la commercialisation des produits locaux et du renforcement des revenus des exploitations familiales. Selon le CNCR, ces discussions ont permis d'identifier des pistes de solutions aux difficultés rencontrées sur le terrain et de faire remonter les préoccupations des producteurs aux autorités. Le Gouvernement promet des ajustements Le CNCR et les organisations paysannes ont salué la démarche de concertation engagée par le Gouvernement, estimant qu'elle s'inscrit dans l'esprit de la Loi d'orientation agro-sylvo-pastorale et halieutique (LOASPH) ainsi que du référentiel Sénégal 2050. À l'issue de la rencontre, le ministre de l'Agriculture s'est engagé à apporter des corrections aux blocages identifiés et à prendre en compte les principales recommandations formulées par les producteurs dans la préparation des prochaines campagnes agricoles. Le CNCR a, de son côté, réaffirmé sa disponibilité à accompagner la mise en œuvre des réformes destinées à promouvoir une agriculture plus performante, résiliente et créatrice de richesses, au service de la souveraineté alimentaire du Sénégal. A.N

items.title: Burkina : Viol aggravé, assassinat, jusqu’à la perpétuité pour 15 condamnés
items.description: À l'issue des audiences foraines des Chambres criminelles du Tribunal de grande instance Ouaga 1, tenue du 20 au 25 juillet 2026, le Procureur du Faso près le Tribunal de grande instance Ouaga 1 porte à la connaissance du public le bilan de cette session. Lisez le communiqué ! Le Procureur du Faso près le Tribunal de Grande Instance Ouaga 1 informe le public que des audiences foraines des chambres criminelle et correctionnelle se sont tenues du 20 au 25 juillet 2026 à la Mairie de Pabré. Ces audiences, tenues simultanément, ont couvert les dossiers de la commune de Pabré, des arrondissements n°03 et n°09 de la ville de Ouagadougou dans le cadre de la politique de rapprochement de la justice des justiciables. En matière criminelle, dix-neuf (19) dossiers impliquant vingt-six (25) personnes étaient inscrits au rôle avec des infractions telles assassinat, meurtre, infanticide, faux et usage de faux en écriture publique, viol aggravé, etc. Dix-huit dossiers ont été jugés. Quinze (15) personnes ont été condamnées avec des peines de soixante (60) mois d’emprisonnement dont douze (12) mois assortis du sursis pour viol aggravé à l’emprisonnement à vie pour assassinat et pour infanticide. Huit (08) mandats d'arrêts ont été décernés. En outre, la chambre criminelle a prononcé,à l'encontre des condamnés, des amendes allant de trois cent mille (300 000) francs CFA ferme à un million (1 000 000) franes CFA ferme. L'ensemble des amendes fermes prononcées s'établit à cinq millions huit cents (5 800 000) francs CFA assorti de contraintes judiciaires à l'exécution. Le taux de traitement des dossiers criminels est à 99 %. En matière correctionnelle, dix-sept (17) dossiers impliquant cinquante-deux (52) prévenus portant sur les infractions de séquestration, d'atteinte à l'intimité de la vie privée, de destruction volontaire de bien immobilier, de stellionat, de coups et blessures volontaires, d'accusation de pratique de sorcellerie, d'escroquerie, de menaces sous condition ont été enrôlés. Seize (16) dossiers ont été jugés. La sanction la plus lourde est de soixante (60) mois d’emprisonnement fermes ainsi qu'à une amende ferme d'un million (1.000.000) francs CFA, pour complicité de séquestration, complicité d'atteinte à l'intimité de la vie privée et pour complicité de coups et blessures volontaires. La peine d’emprisonnement la plus légere est de six (06) mois avec sursis ainsi qu'à une amende de deux cent mille (200 000) francs CFA pour stellionat. Six (06) personnes ont été relaxées pour infractions non constituées ou au bénéfice du doute. Par ailleurs, l'ensemble des amendes prononcées au titre des dossiers correctionnels s'élève à vingt millions trois cent milles (20.300.000) francs CFA assorti de la contrainte judiciaire. Le taux d'exécution des affaires correctionnelles est de 99 %. En marge des audiences, les activités suivantes ont été menées : Délivrance de deux cent quarante-neuf (249) certificats de nationalité burkinabè ; Rectification de soixante-six (66) actes de l'état civil ; Contrôle du centre d'état civil de la commune de Pabré ; Vérification du fonctionnement de l'unité de police judiciaire de Pabré. Le succès de ces audiences foraines est le fruit d'une mobilisation collective exemplaire. Le Procureur du Faso exprime sa profonde gratitude : Au Ministre de la Justice, pour avoir mobilisé les ressources humaines et matérielles indispensables à la tenue de cette mission ; Au Comité International de la Croix Rouge qui a apporté son soutien financier à la tenue de ces audiences ; Au Président de la délégation spéciale de la commune de Pabré dont l'appui logistique et l'engagement aux côtés de la juridiction ont été déterminants pour l'organisation et le bon déroulement des audiences ; Aux Présidents des délégations spéciales des arrondissements n°03 et n°09 pour leur accompagnement dans la tenue effective des audiences ; À l'ensemble des Officiers de Police Judiciaire du ressort, qui ont permis, par leur diligence dans la notification des actes de procédure, la comparution effective des parties et la tenue régulière des audiences dans le respect des délais légaux ; Aux populations de Pabré et des arrondissements n°03 et n°09 de la ville de Ouagadougou et des localités environnantes, pour leur participation massive et leur fort engouement pour les opérations d'état civil et de délivrance de certificats de nationalité. Ces audiences foraines illustrent la volonté résolue de la juridiction de garantir à chaque citoyen, quel que soit son lieu de résidence, un accès effectif à la justice. Le Parquet du Faso réaffirme son engagement à poursuivre cette dynamique au service de la paix sociale et de l'État de droit. Faità Quagadougou, le 25 juillet 2026. Le Procureur du Faso Bakouli Blaise Bazié

items.title: La politique erratique de Trump constitue un frein à la réindustrialisation des États-Unis
items.description: En novembre 2024, Donald Trump avait gagné l’élection présidentielle en s’engageant à réindustrialiser les États-Unis – une part essentielle de sa promesse de « Make America Great Again » (MAGA). Cela lui avait valu en particulier les faveurs de beaucoup de « cols bleus », dont un nombre important de syndiqués, dans les États désindustrialisés qui votaient jusqu’alors traditionnellement démocrate. Ce renouveau industriel aurait dû se concrétiser, au moins en partie, grâce aux droits de douane massifs instaurés dès les premières semaines de son second mandat. Ces mesures étaient censées permettre aux industriels américains de regagner des parts de marché aux États-Unis et obliger les industriels étrangers à y produire s’ils voulaient continuer à y écouler leurs produits. Un an et demi plus tard, on ne constate rien de tel dans les statistiques économiques. L’emploi industriel s’était nettement redressé sous la présidence de Biden après la pandémie du Covid-19, atteignant en 2024 des niveaux que le pays n’avait plus connus depuis la crise de 2008. L’investissement dans la construction de nouvelles usines avait bondi parallèlement : il avait été multiplié par quatre, en dollars courants, entre 2021 et 2024. C’était le résultat notamment des politiques publiques industrielles très actives mises en place par l’administration Biden avec l’Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) ou le Chips Act, qui reposaient sur un important soutien public à l’investissement industriel. Depuis janvier 2025, l’emploi industriel a reculé avec une perte de 75 000 postes , tandis que les investissements dans la construction de nouvelles usines – tout en restant à des niveaux élevés – ont baissé de 85 milliards de dollars par an par rapport au sommet atteint en 2024. L’effet rapide attendu par Trump des mesures protectionnistes massives qu’il a prises ne s’est donc pas traduit pour l’instant dans la réalité. La forte incertitude qui règne désormais sur l’état de droit aux États-Unis, le traitement subi par les immigrants, les tensions politiques et le caractère erratique de la politique de l’administration dans de nombreux domaines n’incitent guère pour l’instant à investir dans le pays. Compte tenu des délais de planification et de lancement de nouvelles usines, qui peuvent aller jusqu’à 10 ans, l'instabilité de la politique de Trump menace la viabilité de nombreux projets. En Ohio, seulement 9 % des industriels relocalisent leur production, notamment car une suppression des tarifs douaniers par une future administration pourrait considérablement en affecter la rentabilité “Liberation Year” has not freed American factories », The Economist , 31 mars 2026.'> 1 . De plus, même pour les entreprises qui décident de relocaliser une partie de leur production aux États-Unis, celles-ci peuvent directement subir les effets des tarifs. C’est notamment le cas pour les entreprises qui ont passé des commandes de machines-outils, soumises à des droits de douane de 25 % par l’administration Trump, comme GE Appliances, dont le régime tarifaire applicable aux produits a changé cinq fois en six mois What happened to the great rebirth of American manufacturing ? », Financial Times , 10 juin 2026. '> 2 . La pénurie de main-d'œuvre, exacerbée par la politique migratoire répressive, pourrait constituer l’obstacle le plus important à une réindustrialisation. Au mois de mai, près de 530 000 emplois étaient à pourvoir dans le secteur manufacturier, soit plus qu’avant la pandémie de Covid-19 Facts About Manufacturing , National Association of Manufacturers.'> 3 .
